title: Why Carney’s pipeline gamble is a bad bet for Canadian taxpayers
gist: Chatham House argues Canada's C$35–44bn publicly-funded oil pipeline and C$4bn LNG support programme is a mispriced bet, because the Asian demand it depends on is already being destroyed by solar and EVs — the IEA's 2018 forecast of +547 TWh Asian gas power by 2025 delivered just 17 TWh, while solar overshot 465 TWh forecast with 1,333 TWh actual. It recommends redirecting the federal balance sheet into smoothing the C$1 trillion grid build-out, where Canada's G7-leading cheap, low-carbon power is an unexploited comparative advantage.

insights.claim: Since taking office in January 2025, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has redirected national energy policy away from emissions reduction and toward increasing fossil fuel exports, reversing the prior Trudeau-era direction.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A policy regime change in a G7 oil exporter: expect Canadian upstream and midstream to trade on subsidy and permitting tailwinds rather than decarbonization discount.
insights.locator: Since taking office in January 2025

insights.claim: The United States buys over 90 per cent of Canada's crude oil exports and practically all of its natural gas exports, making Canadian energy revenue a single-counterparty exposure to a hostile trade partner.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Quantifies the concentration risk that justifies every Canadian export-diversification trade; also caps how much US tariff leverage Ottawa can resist.
insights.locator: Carney took office with a mandate to de-risk Canada

insights.claim: Alberta is responsible for three-quarters of Canadian oil and gas production, which is why federal-provincial friction over energy policy translates directly into national fiscal and political risk.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Alberta's production share means provincial politics, not federal climate policy, is the binding constraint on Canadian supply growth.
insights.locator: relations between Ottawa and Alberta

insights.claim: In July 2026 Alberta and Ottawa agreed a new east-to-west oil pipeline projected to carry 1 million barrels a day of crude along the existing Trans Mountain route, with operations expected to begin only in 2033 or 2034.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A seven-to-eight-year lead time means first oil lands well after the demand-destruction curve the article describes has compounded — timing, not capacity, is the risk.
insights.locator: In July, Alberta and Ottawa agreed a new east-to-west oil pipeline

insights.claim: The new Canadian oil pipeline is expected to cost between C$35 and C$44 billion with most of it borne by the public purse, repeating the funding structure of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A C$35–44bn public capital commitment is a direct sovereign balance-sheet item; watch for cost overruns of the type Trans Mountain already demonstrated.
insights.locator: The new oil pipeline is expected to cost

insights.claim: Canadian federal and provincial support for the LNG build-out is expected to reach C$4 billion by 2031, alongside newly introduced tax breaks incentivizing oil and gas production.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sizes the fiscal subsidy layer supporting Canadian LNG project economics — a policy variable that could reverse with government.
insights.locator: Meanwhile federal and provincial support for the LNG drive

insights.claim: The Alberta secession threat that partly motivates Carney's fossil fuel subsidies is weaker than assumed, with just 18 per cent of Albertans supporting separation in a recent poll.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If the political premium being paid for Alberta's loyalty is based on an overstated secession risk, the subsidy programme is more vulnerable to reversal than markets price.
insights.quote: It is certainly not justified solely by the prospect of Albertan secession, with just 18 per cent of Albertans supporting separation according to one recent poll
insights.locator: The PM should not expose the Canadian taxpayer

insights.claim: Nearly 60 per cent of Canada's oil and gas production is owned by American private equity, meaning public money spent on 'nation-building' export infrastructure largely accrues to US financial owners rather than Canadian ones.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The subsidy's economic beneficiaries are US PE sponsors — a rent transfer that is politically fragile once publicized, and an argument that the strategy fails on its own de-risking terms.
insights.quote: Indeed, nearly 60 per cent of Canada’s oil and gas production is owned by American private equity.
insights.locator: Indeed, nearly 60 per cent of Canada’s oil

insights.claim: LNG Canada is a joint venture of Shell, PETRONAS, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation and the Korean Gas Corporation, so Canada's flagship LNG project is entirely foreign-owned at the equity level.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Exposure to Canadian LNG policy support is best expressed through these listed foreign majors, not through Canadian domestic names.
insights.locator: LNG Canada is a joint venture

insights.claim: Ksi Lisims LNG, a proposed export terminal in British Columbia, is set to be built, owned and operated by wholly-owned subsidiaries of Texas-based Western LNG.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A second Canadian LNG terminal whose operating economics sit with a US sponsor — reinforcing that Canadian export capex does not build Canadian ownership.
insights.locator: Ksi Lisims LNG, a proposed export terminal

insights.claim: Spending Canadian taxpayer money on export infrastructure does not reduce economic risk but merely substitutes dependence on the United States for dependence on other uncertain foreign markets.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The core bear case on Canadian export-led energy policy: the stated de-risking rationale is analytically hollow, which weakens the political durability of the spend.
insights.quote: Pouring taxpayer money into export infrastructure, largely to the benefit of foreign companies, doesn’t de-risk Canada’s economy.
insights.locator: Pouring taxpayer money into export infrastructure

themes.theme: Asian gas demand forecasts have already failed

insights.claim: The IEA's 2018 forecast that gas-fired electricity generation in Asia would grow 547 TWh by 2025 was overshot by a factor of roughly 32x: actual growth was just 17 TWh.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The single most damning datapoint for LNG demand models — institutional Asian gas forecasts have a demonstrated catastrophic upward bias, so haircut every LNG offtake assumption built on them.
insights.quote: In 2018 the IEA predicted that electricity generated by gas in Asia would have grown by 547 TWh by 2025… in fact, it grew by a mere 17 TWh.
insights.locator: Indeed, in 2018 the International Energy Agency (IEA) predicted

insights.claim: The IEA's 2018 estimate that Asian solar generation would grow 465 TWh by 2025 undershot reality by nearly 3x, with actual growth of 1,333 TWh.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The forecast error is directional and symmetric — gas overestimated, solar underestimated — implying consensus energy models still systematically misprice the substitution rate.
insights.quote: In 2018, the IEA estimated solar generation in Asia would grow by 465 TWh by 2025. Instead, it grew by 1,333 TWh
insights.locator: In 2018, the IEA estimated solar generation in Asia

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie estimates only 15 GW of the 53 GW of gas-fired generation capacity planned in Southeast Asia for 2030 will actually be delivered, because of volatile gas prices, financing shortfalls and equipment shortages.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A 72% attrition rate on planned Asian gas capacity is a direct discount to forward LNG offtake — and the causes (financing, turbines) are supply-side, not just price-driven.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie estimates that only 15 GW

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz shock cuts both ways for hydrocarbon exporters: it raises the near-term premium on reliable oil and gas supply while simultaneously accelerating importing nations' shift into renewables and electric transport to insulate against future shocks.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Supply-security shocks that look bullish for LNG in the spot market are structurally bearish for terminal demand — don't extrapolate crisis pricing into 2030s offtake.
insights.locator: It is true that the Strait of Hormuz shock

insights.claim: In China, the largest importer of oil, most new cars sold are already electric, and EV sales in Southeast Asia more than doubled in 2025.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Oil demand destruction is already underway in the marginal buyer Canada is building a pipeline to serve, on a timeline far shorter than the 2033/2034 startup.
insights.locator: In China, the largest importer of oil

insights.claim: The substitution mechanism is direct and compounding: solar panels and batteries destroy demand for gas, EVs destroy demand for oil, and falling demand translates into falling prices for producers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A clean transmission chain from technology deployment to commodity price — use deployment run-rates, not GDP growth, as the leading indicator for long-dated hydrocarbon revenue.
insights.quote: Solar panels and batteries destroy demand for gas. EVs do the same for oil. Falling demand means falling prices.
insights.locator: Solar panels and batteries destroy demand for gas

insights.claim: Under a fast-paced energy transition scenario, value erosion and stranded assets could cost Canada 30 per cent of its oil and gas sector's total value, a loss the taxpayer would substantially bear given the public funding structure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Puts a quantified downside on the sovereign exposure — a 30% sector writedown against C$35–44bn+ of public capital is a fiscal, not just corporate, risk.
insights.locator: Carney’s fossil fuel plans therefore expose Canadian taxpayers

insights.claim: The markets Canada is banking on for export growth will not buy imported oil and gas indefinitely and may cut consumption sooner than currently anticipated, making the demand assumption — not the construction risk — the pipeline's central vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frame Canadian export infrastructure as a duration bet on Asian hydrocarbon demand — the risk is terminal-value collapse, not cost overruns.
insights.quote: The new markets Canada is relying upon for export growth will not buy imported oil and gas forever.
insights.locator: But Carney’s pivot may backfire

insights.claim: Per Natural Resources Canada, Canada has the G7's lowest-cost residential power (2024), second lowest-cost industrial power (2024) and second highest share of non-emitting electricity generation (2023), thanks to a high share of hydro and nuclear.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Cheap clean power is the actual scarce asset in an electricity-constrained global economy — a stronger siting advantage for Canada than any hydrocarbon export terminal.
insights.locator: According to Natural Resources Canada

insights.claim: Montreal's 6 cents per kWh hydro rates attracted C$1.7 billion in AI-related foreign direct investment between 2018 and 2024, demonstrating that cheap low-carbon power already pulls in energy-intensive capital.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A working proof-of-concept for data centre siting economics: power price, not tax policy, is drawing AI capex to Quebec.
insights.locator: Montreal, for example, has cheap hydro rates

insights.claim: Canada's low-emission power mix becomes a compounding trade advantage as markets like the EU increasingly price carbon on imported goods, giving Canadian energy-intensive manufacturing a border-adjustment edge.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Carbon border adjustment turns clean grids into an export subsidy for heavy industry — watch EV manufacturing, critical minerals and green hydrogen siting decisions.
insights.locator: Canada’s low emission power mix is also a strategic advantage

insights.claim: Canada's National Strategy for an Electrified Canadian Economy, launched in May, plans to double the country's electricity system infrastructure, but delivery requires an estimated C$1 trillion by 2050 led by provincial utilities because federal jurisdiction over electricity is limited.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: National Strategy for an Electrified Canadian Economy
insights.so_what: A C$1 trillion multi-decade utility capex cycle with fragmented provincial sponsors — the bottleneck is jurisdiction and financing structure, not policy intent.
insights.locator: A National Strategy for an Electrified Canadian Economy

insights.claim: Because grid investments are recovered as levies on electricity bills, the central risk to Canadian electrification is that upfront capex raises consumer and industrial prices enough to undermine the economic case for switching to electricity in the first place.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A self-defeating feedback loop in rate-base financing — watch retail tariff trajectories as the leading indicator of whether electrification targets hold.
insights.locator: Under current arrangements, these investments will be recovered as levies

insights.claim: A 'Powering Canada Forward Fund' proposed by the Canadian Climate Institute would use the federal balance sheet to hold electricity prices steady while provincial utilities invest, with the public outlay repaid gradually by a growing customer base as consumption rises.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A reusable model for socializing grid capex across time rather than loading it onto today's ratepayers — a template other federations facing load growth may copy.
insights.quote: The federal balance sheet should be used not to underwrite new pipelines, but to ‘smooth’ these predictable electrification costs.
insights.locator: The federal balance sheet should be used

insights.claim: Canada trades more electricity with the United States than it does between its own provinces, so interprovincial transmission is an untapped route to capturing domestic energy value while still exporting surplus power south.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific infrastructure gap where federal money has higher leverage than pipelines — transmission interties, not export terminals.
insights.quote: Canada trades more electricity with the US than it does between provinces
insights.locator: Federal support should also prioritize connecting provincial grids

insights.claim: Electrification offers Canada a double comparative advantage — cheap, low-carbon power that is independent of both Asian and US markets and that benefits every province including Alberta — making it a lower-risk use of public capital than export pipelines.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The article's policy punchline and its political sell: electrification is framed as solving the Alberta problem too, which is what would make a pivot feasible.
insights.quote: Electrification offers a double comparative advantage: cheap, low-carbon power that is independent of Asian and US markets and of benefit to all of Canada – including Alberta.
insights.locator: Electrification offers a double comparative advantage
